A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Adaptive Width Neural Networks. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison. Renaming and appendix reordering can be matched; inconsistent protocol descriptions are assessable document content, rather than missing material.

before.justification: v3 reports original AWNN experiments across tabular, image, sequence, graph, and translation tasks, including Table 1 and appendix analyses. Some graph baseline results are borrowed, but the work's own empirical results are clearly present.

after.justification: v5 retains original experiments and adds real-world tabular results, component ablations, runtime measurements, and neuron-removal analyses.

M1.justification: The quantile-based width updates, importance-rescaled activations, variational objective, and Kaiming+ initialization are retained. AWNN is renamed AWN. The new power-law and sigmoid experiments instantiate importance functions already permitted by v3's framework, without introducing a new training component.

E1.justification: v5 adds pol, MiniBooNE, and credit card clients to the evaluated datasets. This substantially extends tabular coverage from two-dimensional synthetic classification to larger, higher-dimensional real-world problems. The original image, sequence, graph, and translation tasks remain.

E2.justification: Fixed, Fixed+, grid search, random search, local search, Bayesian optimization, and random/magnitude-based truncation comparators are retained. The NAS comparison moves from v3 Appendix L to v5 Appendix J. New width settings and component ablations do not introduce a separate competing method.

E3.justification: Appendix F substantially revises reported sample counts and splits across retained datasets. For example, DoubleMoon changes from 2,500 samples with a 1,750/250/500 outer split to 5,000 with 3,600/400/1,000. New protocols include quantile sweeps, controlled REDDIT-B widths, runtime ratios, and a 5,000-neuron cap in the NoReg ablation. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v5 adds importance-function comparisons, a REDDIT-B width sensitivity study, quantile sensitivity, removal of weight regularization and bounded activations, and individual/cumulative removal of important neurons (Table 2, Appendix H, and Appendices M, N, P). These test substantial additional questions about stability, width control, and neuron importance.

E5.justification: Both versions report Table 1 means and standard deviations over ten final runs and retain the existing fold/configuration averaging practices. Added analyses extend these reporting practices; neither version establishes a new significance-testing procedure, increased repeated-run count, or new seed-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v5 adds tabular accuracies and widths, function-family outcomes, width-sweep results, regularization results, runtimes, and quantile/neuron-removal findings. For example, Table 9 reports MiniBooNE width increasing from 53 to 4,907 under NoReg. Figure 5's random-truncation curve also changes. Original Table 1 and NAS scores remain numerically unchanged despite revised protocol descriptions.

T1.justification: v5 corrects the missing negative exponential signs in Equation 6 and the Gaussian mean expression in Equation 8. It also adds a qualification concerning Folded Normal priors when positive rates are required. The ELBO derivation, Lipschitz proposition, and initialization theorem and proofs are retained.

C1.justification: The principal claims about unbounded width learning, task adaptation, reduced width tuning, and compression remain. One limited strengthening occurs in the introduction: symmetry breaking now asserts that it reduces jostling, whereas v3 said it should do so in principle.

C2.justification: v5 substantially expands practical interpretation: heavy-tailed importance functions allocate more neurons, sigmoid rescaling can impair post-training truncation, and weight regularization helps control width growth. Appendices O and P add interpretations of runtime benefits and remaining neuron redundancy. Section 3.3 also explicitly places adaptive convolutional filters beyond the current formalization.

D1.justification: v5 provides an explicit code-repository address instead of only referring to supplementary material, documents added ablation settings and dataset runtimes, and changes the hardware description from 128 to 64 CPU cores and from 46 to 48 GB per A40. The existing implementation description and principal hyperparameter grids are largely retained.

R1.justification: v5 adds Beyazit et al. (2023) for tabular coverage and discusses relationships to Caron et al. (2025) on asymmetric scaling and Wolinski et al. (2020) on pruning. These are focused additions; the broader positioning relative to constructive methods, NAS, pruning, and unbounded-depth networks remains.

P1.justification: v5 edits the abstract and selected explanatory passages, changes AWNN to AWN, adds a reproducibility section, reorders several appendices, and removes the NeurIPS checklist. The main section sequence and most existing scientific exposition remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: v5 adds four quantitative tables and two multipanel figures covering the new analyses, expands and relocates Table 1, and adopts the ICLR layout. Existing figures and appendix tables are largely retained or relocated, while the added displays substantially broaden the visual presentation of evidence.

improvement.justification: The real-world tabular tests, targeted ablations, runtime measurements, and equation corrections strengthen v5. However, its revised Appendix F splits conflict with retained Section 4 descriptions—for example, 72/8/20 versus 70/10/20 for synthetic data—while the original Table 1 scores remain unchanged. The PDFs do not reconcile which settings underpin those results. These gains coexist with material uncertainty about reproducibility of the central evaluation, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
